## 1. Overview and VM Configuration

I installed Arch Linux on a VMWare Virtual Machine for this assignment meant to make me more comfortable with linux.

Instead of using a graphical installer, I followed the Arch Linux Installation Guide and performed the installation through the command line.

### VM configuration

| Setting | Configuration |
|---|---|
| Operating system | Arch Linux |
| Firmware | UEFI |
| Virtual disk | 30 GB |
| EFI partition | Approximately 1 GiB |
| Root partition | Remaining disk space |
| Bootloader | GRUB |
| Networking | NetworkManager |
| Planned desktop | KDE Plasma |
| Display manager | SDDM |

**Screenshot 1 — VM configuration:** Insert a screenshot of the VM settings showing the virtual disk size and UEFI firmware configuration.

I chose KDE Plasma because I wanted a customizable graphical desktop that would not be too hard to set up. I completed the base installation before moving on to the graphical environment.

## 2. Downloading the Arch Linux ISO

I downloaded the Arch Linux installation files from the official Arch Linux website.

Official resources:

- [Arch Linux Downloads](https://archlinux.org/download/)
- [Arch Linux Installation Guide](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Installation_guide)

### Initial mistake: Downloading the signature file

My first attempt involved using the `.iso.sig` file as though it were the actual installation ISO.

The `.iso` file contains the bootable installation environment. The `.iso.sig` file is a detached cryptographic signature used to verify the authenticity of the ISO; it is not a bootable operating system image and using the mv command to chnage the extension does not change that as I have learned.

**How I fixed it:**

1. Returned to the official Arch Linux download page.
2. Downloaded the actual `.iso` file from a random US mirror.
3. Used the ISO as the virtual machine's installation media.

*Lesson learned:* Pay attention to file extensions, they are probably there for a reason.

## 3. Booting the Live Environment

After attaching the ISO to the VM, I booted into the Arch Linux live environment.

Once the terminal appeared, I checked that the virtual machine had booted successfully.


### Check the system clock

```bash
timedatectl
```

Displays the current time, time zone, and synchronization status.

## 4. Network Configuration and Troubleshooting

Networking was one of the first areas where I encountered confusion.

Initially, I thought I needed to install NetworkManager immediately in the live environment. This led me to attempt a package installation before I understood the distinction between the live installer and the system being installed. Though this attempt to install prematurely somehow fixed the erronious network issues I was having before. (Pings didnt work)

### Test the network

```bash
ping -c 4 archlinux.org
```

I was able to get the ping working, confirming that network connectivity was available.

### Initial NetworkManager installation attempt

```bash
pacman -Syu networkmanager
```

Attempts to synchronize package databases, upgrade packages, and install NetworkManager in the current live environment.

This attempt failed. The live environment uses a limited temporary filesystem, and the installation ran into insufficient overlay space. The problem was not simply that the network was disconnected.


## 5. Partitioning the Virtual Disk

My virtual disk was approximately 30 GB and initially had no partitions.

I used `cfdisk` to create the partition layout.

### Launch the partition editor

```bash
cfdisk /dev/sda
```

Opens the interactive partition editor for `/dev/sda`.

I selected the appropriate GPT partition table and created two partitions:

| Partition | Approximate size | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| `/dev/sda1` | 1 GiB | EFI System Partition |
| `/dev/sda2` | Remaining space | Linux root filesystem |

The EFI partition stores boot files needed by UEFI firmware. The root partition contains the operating system, applications, configuration files, and user data.

After creating the partitions, I wrote the changes to disk and exited `cfdisk`.

### Verify the partition layout

```bash
lsblk
```

Lists block devices and their partitions.


![lsblk](data:image/png;base64,)


## 6. Formatting and Mounting Partitions

After creating the partitions, I formatted them with the appropriate filesystems.

### Format the EFI partition

```bash
mkfs.fat -F 32 /dev/sda1
```

Creates a FAT32 filesystem on the EFI system partition.

### Format the root partition

```bash
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda2
```

Creates an ext4 filesystem on the Linux root partition.


### Mount the root filesystem

```bash
mount /dev/sda2 /mnt
```

Mounts the root partition at `/mnt`, which is the target installation directory.

### Create the boot mount point

```bash
mkdir -p /mnt/boot
```

Creates the directory used for the EFI partition.

### Mount the EFI partition

```bash
mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot
```

Mounts the EFI system partition at `/mnt/boot`.

### Verify the mounts

```bash
lsblk
```

Displays the partition mount points so that I can verify the root and EFI partitions are mounted correctly.

## 7. Installing the Base System

Once the partitions were ready, I installed the core Arch Linux packages into the mounted root filesystem.

```bash
pacstrap -K /mnt base linux linux-firmware networkmanager sudo nano
```

This command installed:

- `base` — the essential Arch Linux system.
- `linux` — the Linux kernel.
- `linux-firmware` — firmware files for supported hardware.
- `networkmanager` — networking management service.
- `sudo` — allows authorized users to execute commands with elevated privileges.
- `nano` — a beginner-friendly terminal text editor.

The `-K` option initializes a keyring for the target installation.

The command completed without errors.

### Generate the filesystem table

```bash
genfstab -U /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab
```

Generates filesystem mount entries using UUIDs and appends them to the target system's `/etc/fstab` file.

This file tells Linux which filesystems should be mounted during boot.

### Verify the generated file

```bash
cat /mnt/etc/fstab
```

Displays the filesystem table for inspection.

*Comment:* This is an important step to remember. If the filesystem table is missing or incorrect, the installed system might not mount its filesystems as expected during startup.

## 8. Configuring the Installed System

After installing the packages, I entered the newly installed system to configure its settings.

### Enter the installed system

```bash
arch-chroot /mnt
```

Changes the apparent root directory to `/mnt`, allowing commands to configure the installed system instead of the live environment.

### Configure the time zone

```bash
ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/America/Chicago /etc/localtime
```

Creates the local time zone link for the Central Time Zone.

```bash
hwclock --systohc
```

Synchronizes the system hardware clock using the current system time.

### Configure the locale

I edited the locale configuration file:

```bash
nano /etc/locale.gen
```

I uncommented the following line:

```text
en_US.UTF-8 UTF-8
```

In Nano, I saved the file and exited.

Then I generated the locale:

```bash
locale-gen
```

Generates the locales enabled in `/etc/locale.gen`.

I also configured the default system locale:

```bash
echo "LANG=en_US.UTF-8" > /etc/locale.conf
```

Sets the default language and character encoding for the system.

### Set the hostname

```bash
echo "archlinux" > /etc/hostname
```

Sets the system hostname to `archlinux`.

I configured the hosts file:

```bash
nano /etc/hosts
```

The relevant entries were:

```text
127.0.0.1   localhost
::1         localhost
127.0.1.1   archlinux.localdomain archlinux
```

These entries provide local hostname resolution.

### Set the root password

```bash
passwd
```

Prompts for a new root password.
I put in a secret passwd

## 9. Installing GRUB

I configured GRUB as the bootloader so the VM could boot into the installed Arch Linux system without relying on the installation ISO.

While still inside the `arch-chroot` environment, I installed the required packages:

```bash
pacman -S grub efibootmgr
```

Installs GRUB and `efibootmgr`, which supports managing UEFI boot entries.

### Install GRUB for UEFI

```bash
grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot --bootloader-id=GRUB
```

Installs the GRUB bootloader for 64-bit UEFI systems using `/boot` as the mounted EFI partition.

### Generate the GRUB configuration

```bash
grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
```

Generates the GRUB configuration file and detects the installed Linux kernel.

### Enable NetworkManager

```bash
systemctl enable NetworkManager
```

Configures NetworkManager to start automatically when the installed system boots.

## 10. Creating Regular Users

After configuring the base system and bootloader, I created a user account for myself and Codi gave both sudo access.

### Create the user

The following is the command format; substitute the username used during my installation.

```bash
useradd -m -G wheel -s /bin/bash Owen
```

```bash
useradd -m -G wheel -s /bin/bash Codi
```

Creates both users with home directories, adds the user to the `wheel` group, and sets Bash as the login shell.

```bash
passwd owen
```

```bash
passwd codi
```
Your pass is `Prof`

### Configure sudo

```bash
EDITOR=nano visudo
```

Opens the sudoers configuration in Nano while using `visudo` to validate the file before saving.

I enabled the appropriate rule for members of the `Sudo` group:

```text
%sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
```

This allows members of `sudo` to run commands as other users, including root, through `sudo`, subject to password authentication and the configured sudo policy. I then added both mine and codi's acc to the sudo group using after making it with groupadd.

```text
groupadd sudo
usermod -aG sudo owen
usermod -aG sudo codi
```


![groups](data:image/png;base64,)


## 11. First Boot and Basic Customization

After finishing the installation, I exited the chroot, unmounted the installed filesystems, and restarted the VM.

### Exit the chroot

```bash
exit
```

Returns to the live installation environment.

### Unmount the installed filesystems

```bash
umount -R /mnt
```

Recursively unmounts filesystems mounted beneath `/mnt`.

### Reboot

```bash
reboot
```

Restarts the VM.

I then booted from the installed virtual disk instead of the installation ISO. The system successfully reached the installed Arch Linux environment, and I was able to log in and use the network.

### Additional shell and system tools

I also worked on basic shell customization and additional tools, including Zsh, OpenSSH, terminal colors, and aliases.

The following are the relevant commands if they match the packages and configuration used in the actual VM.

Install Zsh and OpenSSH:

```bash
sudo pacman -S zsh openssh
```

Installs the Zsh shell and OpenSSH tools.

Set Zsh as the default shell for the current user:

```bash
chsh -s /bin/zsh
```

Changes the current user's default login shell. A new login may be required before the change takes effect.

Enable the SSH service:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable sshd
```

Configures the SSH server to start automatically at boot.


## 12. Installing KDE Plasma

I chose KDE Plasma because I wanted a visually appealing, customizable graphical desktop.

### Update the system

```bash
sudo pacman -Syu
```

Synchronizes package databases and upgrades installed packages. Prob not needed but better safe than sorry.

### Install KDE Plasma

```bash
sudo pacman -S plasma-meta konsole dolphin
```

Installs the Plasma desktop package group, Konsole terminal emulator, and Dolphin file manager. The package group may pull in additional dependencies.

### Install and enable SDDM

```bash
sudo pacman -S sddm
```

Installs the Simple Desktop Display Manager, which provides the graphical login screen.

```bash
sudo systemctl enable sddm
```

Enables SDDM to start automatically at boot.

After installation, reboot:

```bash
sudo reboot
```
